definition: A long-horizon estimate of the power price at which developers would be willing to build new generation, used as an implied ceiling for future power prices.
core_idea: LCOE is calculated by dividing the cost of building a generating unit by its expected generation volume, adjusted for the time value of money, and can be extended to include fixed and variable operating costs (fuel, maintenance, overhead); if market prices rise above this level, new entry should occur and push prices back down.
key_points: Provides an estimated upper bound for long-horizon power prices
Basic version divides build cost by time-value-adjusted expected generation volume; can be expanded to include fixed and variable operating costs
Common uses: PPA pricing, fundamental forecasts, capacity market pricing, renewable energy certificate market analysis
Also used to compare competitiveness across different generating technologies over a typical life span and duty cycle
Key input is the cost of new entry (CONE), the estimated cost to construct a new unit
CONE is spread across the facility's expected life using discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis to derive a daily revenue requirement in $/MW-day
The underlying math is analogous to annuity calculations used in finance
relationships: Depends on CONE and DCF/annuity math
Used in capacity markets and PPA pricing
trading_implications: Serves as a fundamental, long-run reference point for where power prices should cap out, informing long-horizon forecasts
